newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin "not pessimistic" after meeting over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Jospin "not pessimistic" after meeting over Europe.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Saturday he was "not pessimistic" about the outcome of a European Union summit next week in Amsterdam which will centre on how to proceed towards a single currency.
Jospin spoke after a two-hour encounter with President Jacques Chirac, whose office said it had been "a good meeting."
A Chirac aide said the meeting had "allowed France's position to be defined...ahead of Amsterdam."
Jospin told reporters a wide series of European issues was discussed.
The meeting, attended by key cabinet members, was called after a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, failed on Friday to resolve differences on a single currency.

France's new Socialist-led government, which swept to power in an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1, raised its objections to the pact leading to a single currency for the first time last week.
Jospin wants the EU to put employment as high on its list of priorties as monetary stability.
He arrived at the Elysee palace with Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn and European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici.
The French leaders were to discuss further steps, with Europe now facing an uphill task to strike a deal on an EU budget stability pact in time for the summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.
Strauss-Kahn told reporters earlier in the day that reaching agreement with Germany at the summit would be hard but that progress was being made.
"The Germans have understood they must make a step forward if they want things to advance and we have to do the same," he said.

"Mutual concessions are the very definition of co-operation between two countries. I have the impression things are moving -- it's difficult, but things are moving and I hope we will reach agreement in Amsterdam," Strauss-Kahn said.
Jospin said in Poitiers the new government was committed to a single currency but wanted a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.
Demands for a focus on growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of a single currency, he said.
Aides quoted Jospin as having told the Socialist meeting in Paris, mostly devoted to domestic issues, that he would not accept a simple "social addendum" to the stability treaty.

Jospin told the meeting he believed he was speaking for other European peoples and not only for his own, when he said growth, development, employment and the fight against inequality should have equal footing as a priority with monetary stability in the pact.

Socialist first secretary Francois Hollande told reporters Jospin wanted the EU to revive a project it had approved, but never acted upon, to create hundreds of thousands of jobs across western Europe by launching major public works projects, especially connected with transport.
The plan, adoped at a summit in Essen, Germany, in 1994 included new EU-financed highways and high-speed railway lines.
France's new government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1, raised its objections to the pact for the first time on Monday.
Both France and Germany are keen to avoid any suggestion of a rift between Paris and Bonn, whose alliance is seen as crucial to pushing monetary union through in 1999.
